title: The Peter Principle (Rising To Your Level Of Incompetence)
description: In a hierarchy, people are promoted based on their performance in their current role. They keep getting promoted until they reach a role where they are no longer competent—and there they stay. The organization fills with people who are one level above their ability.
shortDescription: In a hierarchy, people are promoted based on their performance in their current role. They keep getting promoted until they reach a role where they are no longer competent—and there they stay. The organization fills with people who are one level above their ability.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: In a hierarchy, people are promoted based on their performance in their current role. They keep getting promoted until they reach a role where they are no longer competent—and there they stay. The organization fills with people who are one level above their ability.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: The brilliant engineer who becomes a terrible manager.
The top salesperson who, as sales director, destroys the team.
The teacher who becomes a principal and is miserable and ineffective because the skills don’t transfer.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: The promoted person clings to their old skills (the engineer who micromanages code instead of leading people).
They are stressed, overwhelmed, and blame external factors.
They stop learning because they feel they should already know everything.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I was great in my last role; this new role just isn’t set up for success.”
“I don’t have time for strategy; I’m too busy doing the real work.”
“They’re not performing because they don’t work as hard as I did.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: A manager was promoted because they were the best individual contributor, not because they showed leadership potential.
The person’s new responsibilities are a mismatch for their core skills.
They’ve stopped growing and become a bottleneck.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Laurence J. Peter observed this in 1969. Organizations reward competence with promotion into a different kind of work, assuming that skill at one level implies skill at the next. It’s a structural flaw, not a personal one.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: For yourself: before accepting a promotion, shadow someone in that role and honestly assess whether the skills match.
For organizations: create expert tracks (promotion without management) so people aren’t forced into roles they’ll fail at.
If you’re above your level of competence, be honest and seek a lateral move back to where you thrived.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming that someone who is bad at their job is lazy. They may be in the wrong job entirely.
Promoting your best people into management as a default reward, without checking whether they want it or can do it.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A brilliant software developer is promoted to team lead. She hates meetings, struggles with giving feedback, and misses coding. Her team’s morale drops, and she becomes depressed. The company loses a great developer and gains a terrible manager. A dual‑track promotion system would have kept her coding and made her a technical fellow, not a people manager.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Promotion is not a reward; it’s a different job. The staircase to success sometimes leads to a room you don’t belong in.
